report.source_text: At the emergency room, the patient Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 (eyes 4, verbal 4, motor 6) as he was awake, not in pain or distress, tracking examiner and following simple commands. He knew the month and year as well as his name, age and date of birth. His speech was clear, and he was aware of being in a hospital but could not name the president. He had decreased attention and did not cooperate for aphasia testing. He was slightly impulsive, trying to pull out the lines and leads connected to him. No findings suggestive of gaze or face palsy were found, and motor strength testing was intact.

clinician.final_diagnosis: This case presentation is about a patient with COVID-19 who presented with encephalopathy without respiratory symptoms or focal findings who developed PRES during hospitalisation.
clinician.trajectory_summary: An 85-year-old man with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, diabetes, CKD, and hypertension presented with acute encephalopathy (odd behavior, decreased attention, impulsivity) and a positive SARS-CoV-2 molecular assay. Initial neurological exam showed no focal deficits. Initial head CT and a limited brain MRI (DWI/ADC) were negative for acute findings. Initial labs showed thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, lactate, and troponin. On the second night of admission, the patient's mental status deteriorated, becoming drowsy with decreased verbal output. A repeat head CT hours after this deterioration showed new regions of decreased density in the right cerebellar hemisphere and bilateral subcortical occipital lobe regions, which were confirmed by another CT 24 hours later. An EEG showed generalized slowing. A repeat brain MRI on day 12 post-admission was normal, without FLAIR abnormality or contrast enhancement, suggesting resolution of the imaging findings.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with odd behavior, impaired attention, and impulsivity, consistent with encephalopathy.
Initial neurological examination showed no focal deficits (no gaze or face palsy, intact motor strength).
Patient experienced neurological deterioration on the second night of admission, becoming drowsy and unresponsive to commands.

Repeat head CT hours after neurological deterioration showed new regions of decreased density in the right cerebellar hemisphere and bilateral subcortical occipital lobe regions, consistent with PRES.
These CT findings were confirmed by another head CT 24 hours later.
EEG after deterioration showed generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges.
Brain MRI on day 12 post-admission was normal, without FLAIR abnormality or contrast enhancement, indicating resolution of findings.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Acute stroke or hemorrhage as cause of initial encephalopathy or later deterioration
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Initial head CT was negative for acute findings (E004). Early MRI DWI/ADC sequences were negative (E005). The later CT findings of decreased density in specific regions, followed by resolution on MRI, are more consistent with PRES than stroke.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: EEG showed generalized slowing but no epileptiform discharges (E009).
